title: Newborn life support
blurb: Support a newborn's transition and resuscitate using the RCUK 2025 algorithm: warmth, airway, inflation breaths at the right pressure and oxygen, ventilation, compressions at 3:1 and adrenaline.
question: Baby Ola is born at 39 weeks at a midwife-led unit. He is floppy, not breathing and his heart rate is about 50 beats per minute. After drying and opening the airway, what should the midwife give first?

teach.body: Formally (Resuscitation Council UK 2025, newborn resuscitation and support of transition of infants at birth): most newborns need only warmth, drying and time; a few need help to inflate their lungs, and very few need compressions or drugs. In plain English: a newborn who is not breathing is almost always short of air in the lungs, not suffering a primary heart problem. So the airway and lung inflation come first: without lung inflation, chest compressions will be ineffective.

teach.h: Thermal care and the first assessment
items: Keep the newborn's temperature 36.5 to 37.5°C. Delivery room 23 to 25°C (over 28 weeks).
32 weeks or more: dry immediately, remove wet towels, put on a hat. Under 32 weeks: dry the head, hat, body into a plastic bag without drying.
Aim for delayed cord clamping of 60 seconds or more while assessing, ideally after the lungs are inflated.
Assess breathing, heart rate (stethoscope at first) and tone. Stimulate gently by drying and rubbing the back or soles.
Do not use skin colour to judge oxygenation. Reassess breathing and heart rate every 30 seconds.

steps.label: Dry, warm, assess
steps.sub: Breathing, HR, tone; call for help

steps.label: Compressions 3:1
steps.sub: If HR under 60 after 30 s effective ventilation

teach.caption: Start respiratory support if the baby is not breathing regularly or the heart rate is under 100 per minute.

teach.h: Term and preterm: the numbers differ
teach.caption: RCUK 2025. NICE NG235 also advises starting basic resuscitation of term babies in air.

teach.h: No chest rise? Fix the airway before anything else
teach.body: Visible chest movement shows the airway is open and volume is delivered. If the chest does not rise: reposition the head, reapply the mask and repeat 5 inflations; use two-person jaw thrust or a supraglottic airway; then consider a higher inflation pressure. Once the chest rises, give ventilation breaths at 30 per minute (15 over 30 seconds) and reassess the heart rate every 30 seconds.

items.label: HR after at least 30 s of effective ventilation: start compressions
adrenaline IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of 1:10,000), every 4 min

teach.caption: Two-thumb encircling technique, one-third of the chest depth. Stop compressions when HR is over 60. Sodium bicarbonate was removed in 2025.

head: Time from birth
Target SpO2
teach.caption: Avoid SpO2 under 80% and/or bradycardia at 5 minutes; reduce oxygen if saturations exceed 95%.

teach.h: Scenario: baby Ola at the midwife-led unit
items: Ola is floppy, apnoeic, HR about 50. The midwife calls for help (second midwife, 999 for transfer) and dries and wraps him under the heater.
She opens the airway in a neutral position and gives 5 inflation breaths of 2-3 seconds at 30 cm H2O in air.
No chest rise: she repositions, uses two-person jaw thrust with her colleague and repeats 5 inflations. Now the chest rises.
She gives ventilation breaths at 30 per minute. After 30 seconds of effective ventilation the HR is 110 and rising, so no compressions are needed.
A colleague supports the parents and records times; Ola transfers with a midwife for neonatal review.

teach.text: Don't jump to chest compressions because the heart rate is low at birth. The trigger is a heart rate under 60 AFTER at least 30 seconds of effective ventilation with visible chest rise. And the newborn ratio is 3:1, not the adult 30:2 or the paediatric 15:2.

items: Warmth first: 36.5-37.5°C; under 32 weeks into a plastic bag without drying.
5 inflation breaths of 2-3 s: 30 cm H2O and air (32 weeks+), 25 cm H2O and 30% oxygen or more (under 32 weeks).
No chest rise: reposition, two-person jaw thrust, supraglottic airway, then higher pressure.
Compressions if HR under 60 after 30 s of effective ventilation: 3:1, 100% oxygen.
Adrenaline 20 micrograms/kg IV/IO every 4 minutes; no sodium bicarbonate.

summary: You can now support a newborn's transition with thermal care and assessment, and run the RCUK 2025 newborn algorithm from airway and inflation breaths to ventilation, compressions and adrenaline. You can also adjust pressures and oxygen for babies under 32 weeks and use saturation targets.

A.q: A term baby is not breathing after drying and stimulation. The midwife opens the airway. What starting inflation pressure does RCUK 2025 recommend?
A.why: RCUK 2025: for infants of 32 weeks or more, start inflation breaths at 30 cm H2O.

whyNot.0: 20 cm H2O is below both RCUK starting pressures.
whyNot.1: 25 cm H2O is the starting pressure for infants under 32 weeks.
whyNot.3: 40 cm H2O is not a starting pressure; higher pressures are considered only if the chest does not rise.

A.q: A baby born at 29 weeks needs inflation breaths. What concentration of oxygen should resuscitation start with?
A.why: RCUK 2025: start in 21% oxygen at 32 weeks or more, and 30% or more under 32 weeks.

whyNot.0: Air (21%) is the starting gas for babies of 32 weeks or more.
whyNot.2: 60% is not the RCUK starting concentration.
whyNot.3: 100% oxygen is used once chest compressions start, not at the outset.

A.q: A newborn's heart rate is 50 per minute after 30 seconds of effective ventilation with good chest rise. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should be used?
A.why: RCUK 2025: newborn compressions use a 3:1 synchronised ratio, aiming for 90 compressions and 30 ventilations per minute.

whyNot.1: 15:2 is the paediatric ratio for infants and children beyond the newborn period.
whyNot.3: 5:1 is not a recommended newborn ratio.

B.q: A midwife gives 5 inflation breaths to an apnoeic term newborn but sees no chest rise. What should she do next?
options: Reposition the airway and repeat inflations
B.why: RCUK 2025: if there is no chest rise, reposition, reapply the mask and repeat 5 inflations, using alternative airway manoeuvres if needed.

whyNot.0: Without lung inflation, chest compressions will be ineffective.
whyNot.1: Drugs are considered only after effective ventilation and compressions have failed.
whyNot.3: Oxygen cannot reach the lungs until the airway is open and the chest rises.

B.q: A baby is born at 30 weeks. Which thermal care is recommended immediately after birth?
options: Dry fully, then wrap in warm towels
Bath in warm water to raise temperature
Skin-to-skin after drying the whole body
Plastic bag without drying, plus a hat
B.why: RCUK 2025: under 32 weeks, dry the head and put on a hat, and place the body in a plastic (polyethene) bag without drying.

whyNot.0: Drying and towels is the approach for babies of 32 weeks or more.
whyNot.1: Bathing causes heat loss and has no place in immediate newborn thermal care.
whyNot.2: This preterm baby needs the plastic bag approach; drying the body increases heat loss.

B.q: During newborn resuscitation, when should chest compressions be stopped?
options: When the heart rate is over 60
When the heart rate is over 100
B.why: RCUK 2025: discontinue chest compressions once the heart rate is over 60 per minute, continuing ventilation as needed.

whyNot.1: Ventilation continues until HR is over 100 and breathing is adequate, but compressions stop once HR is over 60.
whyNot.2: There is no fixed number of cycles; the heart rate guides the decision.
whyNot.3: RCUK advises not to use skin colour to assess oxygenation.

C.q: A term baby at a home birth has HR 80 and gasping breaths after drying. Inflation breaths produced chest rise. Ventilation breaths are now under way. How often should they be given?
C.why: RCUK 2025: after successful inflations give ventilation breaths, 15 over 30 seconds (30 per minute) with an inflation time of about 1 second.

whyNot.0: 40 to 60 per minute is faster than the RCUK ventilation rate.
whyNot.2: 12 to 20 per minute is well below the RCUK newborn ventilation rate of 30 per minute.
whyNot.3: 90 per minute is the number of compressions during 3:1 CPR, not the ventilation rate.

C.q: Despite effective ventilation and 3:1 compressions with 100% oxygen, a term baby's heart rate remains under 60. Which drug and dose is recommended?
C.why: RCUK 2025: adrenaline 20 micrograms/kg IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of 1:10,000), UVC preferred, repeated every 4 minutes.

whyNot.1: Sodium bicarbonate was removed from the newborn algorithm in 2025.
whyNot.2: 1 mg IM is an adult dose and route, not the newborn regimen.
whyNot.3: Glucose (200 mg/kg, 2 mL/kg of 10%) is given if glucose is low; it does not treat bradycardia in arrest.

C.q: At 5 minutes after birth, a term baby receiving ventilation has a right-hand SpO2 of 72% and HR 140. What should the midwife do with the oxygen?
options: Turn the oxygen down to air
C.why: RCUK 2025: target SpO2 at 5 minutes is 80-85% and SpO2 under 80% at 5 minutes should be avoided, so titrate oxygen upwards.

whyNot.0: 72% is below the 5-minute target of 80-85%, so oxygen needs adjusting.
whyNot.1: Reducing oxygen is for saturations over 95%.
whyNot.3: The baby still needs support while saturations are below target.

reteach.title: Air first, then heart
reteach.question: If a newborn's heart is slow because the lungs are full of fluid and there is no oxygen, what is the fastest way to speed it up?

blocks.h: Inflate the lungs and the heart follows
blocks.body: In most babies who need help at birth, the heart is slow because of low oxygen. Opening the airway and inflating the lungs (long 2-3 second breaths) replaces the fluid with air; oxygen then reaches the heart and the rate rises. That is why the chest must be seen to rise before anything else. Compressions and adrenaline are for the small number whose heart rate stays under 60 despite good ventilation.

children.edge: Chest rises, HR under 60 after 30 s
children.label: Compressions 3:1, 100% O2

blocks.text: Inflation breaths are long (2-3 seconds, 5 of them); ventilation breaths are short (about 1 second, 30 per minute). Mixing them up is a common error.

explain.body: Keep the baby at 36.5-37.5°C. Assess breathing, heart rate and tone, and reassess every 30 seconds. Stimulate gently. Delay cord clamping 60 seconds or more where possible (RCUK 2025).

test.q: What temperature range does RCUK 2025 advise for a newborn during stabilisation?
test.why: RCUK 2025: maintain newborn temperature between 36.5 and 37.5°C.

whyNot.0: This range is below the target and represents hypothermia.
whyNot.1: 36.0°C is below the lower limit of the RCUK range.
whyNot.2: 38.0°C is above the upper limit; overheating should also be avoided.

explain.body: Neutral head position, jaw thrust (two-person is more effective). 5 inflation breaths of 2-3 seconds at 30 cm H2O in air (32 weeks+) or 25 cm H2O in 30% or more oxygen (under 32 weeks). Look for chest rise.

test.q: How long should each newborn inflation breath last?
test.why: RCUK 2025: give 5 inflation breaths with an inflation time of 2-3 seconds.

whyNot.0: About 1 second is the inflation time for ventilation breaths, not inflation breaths.
whyNot.1: 0.5 seconds is too short to clear lung fluid.
whyNot.3: 5 seconds is longer than the RCUK inflation time.

explain.body: Start if HR is under 60 after at least 30 seconds of effective ventilation. Increase oxygen to 100%, call experienced help, two-thumb encircling, one-third of chest depth, 3:1. Stop when HR is over 60.

test.q: When starting newborn chest compressions, what should happen to the inspired oxygen?
options: Reduce it to protect the eyes
test.why: RCUK 2025: when starting chest compressions, increase oxygen to 100%.

whyNot.1: Air is the starting gas for term inflation, not during compressions.
whyNot.2: 30% is the starting gas for preterm inflation, not during compressions.
whyNot.3: Oxygen is increased, not reduced, when compressions begin.

explain.body: Adrenaline 20 micrograms/kg IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of 1:10,000), UVC preferred, every 4 minutes. Glucose 200 mg/kg if low. No sodium bicarbonate. Target SpO2 80-85% at 5 minutes and 85-95% at 10 minutes.

test.q: How often can intravenous adrenaline be repeated during newborn resuscitation under RCUK 2025?
test.why: RCUK 2025 simplified adrenaline timing to every 4 minutes.

whyNot.0: Every 2 minutes is more frequent than the RCUK 2025 interval.
whyNot.2: Every 10 minutes is less frequent than recommended.
whyNot.3: 30 seconds is the interval for reassessing heart rate, not for repeating adrenaline.
